prime.problem: Quicksort can hit n², and merge sort needs an n-element buffer. If memory is fixed and n² is unacceptable, you need a sort that is O(n log n) on every input using only the array itself.
prime.fits: Uses cs-1's binary heap as a sorting engine. It's the fallback inside introsort (quicksort card) and the in-place, unstable row of the n log n card's table.
expect: array as a tree: children at 2i + 1, 2i + 2
swap max to the end, shrink
prime.goal: Trace build-heap and the extract phase, prove the build is O(n), and say when heapsort's guarantee is worth its 3× slowdown.

attend: Why does the build phase start sifting at index n // 2 − 1 and go backwards?
Why is building the heap O(n) when each sift-down can cost log n?
After swapping the max to the end, why is only the root possibly out of place?
How do two equal keys end up reversed, as in [2a, 2b] → [2b, 2a]?
Why is heapsort 3.1× slower than introsort in numpy even though both run in C?

must: Max-heap: every parent ≥ its children → the max is at a[0] → swap it to the last slot, shrink the heap by one → only the new root breaks the heap → one sift-down (≤ log₂ n levels) repairs it → n − 1 extractions give O(n log n) on every input

Sift-down costs at most a node's height, and most nodes are near the bottom (half are leaves) → Σ heights = n − popcount(n) < n → build-heap is O(n) (999,993 for 10⁶ vs n log₂ n ≈ 19.9 M) → pushing one at a time with sift-up is O(n log n) because the many deep nodes walk far
Heap and sorted tail share one array → O(1) extra space and no bad inputs → the only sort with both, which is why introsort falls back to it → but long-distance swaps make it unstable
elevated: Sift-down jumps from i to 2i + 1 → at n = 10⁶ about 20 levels, most on different cache lines → 0.096 s vs introsort's sequential 0.031 s (our reading of the gap, not measured directly)
reference: the source's single combined while loop
the n − popcount(n) identity checked up to 3,000
the 8 MB buffer figure for merge sort

compress.prompt: From memory, write heapsort as two phases in 3–4 sentences: what build-heap does and why it's O(n), what each extraction does and why it's O(log n), and the two properties it gives up.
checklist: view the array as a complete binary tree via 2i + 1 and 2i + 2
build: sift down every internal node, last first; O(n) because heights sum to less than n
extract: swap max to the end, shrink, sift the root down; log n each
O(n log n) worst case, O(1) extra space
not stable; poor cache behaviour, so slower than quicksort in practice

retrieve.q: Explain why build-heap is O(n) but inserting n items one by one with sift-up is O(n log n), even though both produce a heap.
answer: sift-down costs a node's height; most nodes are leaves or near them, so the heights sum to less than n
sift-up costs a node's depth; most nodes are deep, so the depths sum to about n log n
same result, but the work lands on the few top nodes in one case and the many bottom nodes in the other

retrieve.q: Walk through the first extraction on the heap [82, 27, 43, 3, 9, 38, 10]: what is swapped, which comparisons happen during the sift-down, and what is the array after?
answer: swap 82 with a[6] = 10; the heap is now indices 0–5
root 10: bigger child is 43 (vs 27) → swap; at index 2, bigger child 38 → swap

retrieve.q: An embedded controller sorts sensor readings in a fixed 4 KB buffer with a hard deadline. Heapsort, quicksort or merge sort, and what are you giving up?
answer: heapsort: O(n log n) worst case in O(1) extra space, so the deadline and memory both hold
quicksort risks n² on unlucky input; merge sort needs a second buffer
you give up stability and some average-case speed (cache misses)

compare.q: The heaps card uses a heap as a priority queue; this card uses it to sort. What is the same, and what does sorting in place change about how the heap is built and used?
answer: same: the heap property and sift-down/sift-up on an array
a priority queue grows by pushes (sift-up); heapsort builds all at once bottom-up (O(n))
heapsort uses a max-heap and parks each extracted max in the freed slot at the end, so no extra array is needed

compare.q: Both guarantee O(n log n). Which design choice gives merge sort stability and heapsort O(1) space, and what does each cost in practice?
answer: merge sort writes into a separate buffer, taking ties from the left: stable, O(n) space
heapsort swaps inside the array across long distances: in place, unstable
merge sort costs memory (8 MB for 10⁶ floats); heapsort costs cache misses (0.096 s vs 0.072 s)

predict.q: Building a max-heap from an already-sorted ascending array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]: predict whether it needs many swaps or few, and why.
predict.answer: Many, close to the maximum. Ascending order puts the smallest values at the top, so every internal node must sink as far as it can: 3 sinks 1 level, 2 sinks 1, and 1 sinks 2, 4 swaps, which is the n = 7 height bound (2 + 1 + 1). A descending array is already a max-heap and needs 0 swaps. So heapsort's build is cheapest on reverse-sorted input, the opposite of insertion sort.

apply.task: Build a max-heap from [4, 10, 3, 5, 1] by hand: sift i = 1, then i = 0, drawing the tree after each. Count comparisons. Then check the sum-of-heights identity for n = 10.
apply.done: The heap is [10, 5, 3, 4, 1], the build made 6 comparisons, and for n = 10 the heights sum to 8 = 10 − 2 (10 is 1010 in binary: two 1 bits).
apply.hint: i = 1 holds 10, already bigger than its children 5 and 1 (2 comparisons, 0 swaps). Then 4 at the root sinks twice.
